claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a homogeneous high-temperature BCC alloy.
Phase stability during cooling of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by the Gibbs free-energy difference between BCC and FCC.
The BCC–FCC Gibbs free-energy difference controls the kinetic barrier to transformation.
A larger driving force associated with destabilized BCC produces a faster and more complete BCC-to-FCC or mixed-phase transformation.
Minor compositional changes, such as increasing Co, can modify the BCC–FCC Gibbs free-energy difference.
Samples can be compared under identical cooling rates and thermal profiles to isolate the effect of composition.
Atomic diffusion becomes active below the critical transformation temperature.
Evolving BCC and FCC phase fractions can be tracked using XRD, EBSD, and TEM.
Phase-fraction evolution mediates the proposed connection between thermodynamic driving force and microstructural change.
Increasing the BCC-to-FCC driving force decreases BCC stability.
Increasing the BCC-to-FCC driving force reduces the kinetic activation barrier.
A reduced kinetic barrier accelerates nucleation and growth of FCC during cooling.
A slight increase in Co will heighten the driving force for BCC-to-FCC transformation.
Co-enriched samples will transform from BCC to FCC faster and more completely than baseline Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Baseline Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will transform at a moderate rate under the selected cooling or aging treatment.
The prediction applies only where diffusion is sufficiently active and may be obscured by oxidation or severe compositional heterogeneity.
CALPHAD-based design and prior experiments support a qualitative association among Gibbs free-energy difference, phase stability, and transformation rate.
The quantitative relation and any critical driving-force threshold remain uncertain because of compositional fluctuations and diffusion barriers.
Failure of the Co-modified samples to show statistically significant acceleration relative to the identically treated baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
